note: Tlaxcala, the Totonac lands and the ground the Spaniards and their allies held are drawn as occupied areas, and moving circles mark Cortés's army on the march. Areas and routes are approximate.
dataNote: The Aztec Empire is drawn from the base map. Areas and routes are approximate reconstructions from the chronicles and campaign maps.

chapters.title: Landing on the Gulf coast
chapters.text: Cortés's eleven ships anchored off San Juan de Ulúa, and on 22 April 1519 his men came ashore. Moctezuma's envoys brought rich gifts, hoping the strangers would leave. Instead Cortés founded the town of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz and won over the Totonacs of Cempoala, who were tired of paying tribute to the Aztecs.

chapters.title: Tlaxcala and Cholula
arrows: Cortés enters Tlaxcala as an ally (September 1519)
Cortés and the Tlaxcalans march to Cholula (October 1519)
chapters.text: Climbing onto the plateau, the Spaniards and their Totonac allies fought the Tlaxcalans from 2 to 5 September 1519. Tlaxcala, surrounded by the Aztec Empire but never conquered by it, then chose to ally with them, a decision that shaped the whole war. At Cholula, an Aztec tributary, Cortés and his Tlaxcalan allies massacred the city's nobles on 18 October, and pro-Tlaxcalan leaders took over.

chapters.title: Moctezuma's guests and captors
arrows: Cortés crosses the pass between the volcanoes to Tenochtitlan (November 1519)
Cortés hurries to the coast against Narváez (May 1520)
chapters.text: Moctezuma welcomed Cortés into Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519 and lodged the Spaniards in his father's palace; within days they made him their prisoner. In May 1520 Cortés marched back to the coast and defeated Pánfilo de Narváez, sent from Cuba to arrest him, at Cempoala. Meanwhile Pedro de Alvarado massacred Aztec nobles at a festival, and the city rose against the Spaniards.

chapters.title: La Noche Triste and Otumba
arrows: Cortés returns to Tenochtitlan with Narváez's men (June 1520)
La Noche Triste: the breakout along the Tlacopan causeway (30 June 1520)
The retreat round the northern lakes to Otumba and Tlaxcala (July 1520)
chapters.text: Cortés returned on 24 June 1520 to a city in revolt, and Moctezuma was killed days later. On the night of 30 June the Spaniards and Tlaxcalans broke out along the causeway to Tlacopan, losing hundreds of Spaniards and thousands of allies. They fled round the northern lakes, beat off a great Aztec army at Otumba on 7 July and found refuge in Tlaxcala.

chapters.title: Regrouping in Tlaxcala
chapters.text: Tlaxcala refused Aztec offers and kept its alliance with Cortés. From August 1520 Spaniards and Tlaxcalans attacked Tepeaca, an Aztec tributary that had killed Spaniards, and it became an allied town. That autumn smallpox swept through the Valley of Mexico and killed the new emperor, Cuitláhuac, on 4 December.

chapters.title: Texcoco and the lakeshore
arrows: Cortés marches from Tlaxcala to Texcoco (December 1520)
Raid round the northern lakes to Xaltocan and Tlacopan (February 1521)
Cortés circles the southern and western lakes by Xochimilco (April 1521)
chapters.text: At the end of December 1520 Cortés led his Spaniards and more than 10,000 Tlaxcalans into the Valley of Mexico and made Texcoco, on the eastern shore of the lake, his base. Chalco and other lakeside towns came over to him early in 1521. He raided round the lakes, fighting at Xochimilco in April, while thirteen brigantines were built for the attack on the island city.

chapters.title: The siege and fall of Tenochtitlan
arrows: Alvarado's column takes post at Tlacopan (May 1521)
Olid's column takes post at Coyoacán (May 1521)
Sandoval's column takes post at Iztapalapa (May 1521)
Cortés's thirteen brigantines sweep the lake (late May – June 1521)
The final advance into Tlatelolco (July – August 1521)
chapters.text: In late May 1521 three columns took post at Tlacopan, Coyoacán and Iztapalapa and cut the aqueduct from Chapultepec, and the brigantines won control of the lake. The besiegers advanced along the causeways, razing each district they took, and by the start of August they had reached the market of Tlatelolco. On 13 August Cuauhtémoc was captured as he tried to escape by canoe, and the starving city surrendered.

battles.name: Cholula massacre
battles.casualties: About 3,000 Cholulans killed by Cortés's own count, 6,000 by Gómara's; one witness claimed up to 30,000

battles.name: Battle of Cempoala (Cortés against Narváez)
battles.casualties: About 17 killed: 15 of Narváez's men and 2 of Cortés's

battles.name: La Noche Triste
battles.casualties: About 800–1,200 Spaniards and 1,000–4,000 Tlaxcalans killed, drowned or captured (accounts vary widely); Aztec losses unknown

battles.name: Battle of Otumba
battles.casualties: About 60 Spaniards killed; Tlaxcalan and Aztec losses unknown

battles.name: Siege of Tenochtitlan
battles.casualties: An estimated 100,000 Aztec warriors and at least 40,000 civilians killed or captured (some estimates up to 240,000 dead); 450–860 Spaniards and about 20,000 Indigenous allies
